\\\"references/S-TORCH-NUMERIC/fulltext.txt\\\", \\\"sha256\\\": \\\"bb6b2d8154a10f8f3b15e5ae4465cbc8d833067046964fc6b4d66dc036131b45\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"source_original\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"\\\\n===== docs/source/notes/numerical_accuracy.rst =====\\\\n.. _numerical_accuracy:\\\\n\\\\nNumerical accuracy\\\\n==================\\\\n\\\\nIn modern computers, floating point numbers are represented using IEEE 754 standard.\\\\nFor more details on floating point arithmetic and IEEE 754 standard, please see\\\\n`Floating point arithmetic <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating-point_arithmetic>`_\\\\nIn particular, note that floating point provides limited accuracy (about 7 decimal digits\\\\nfor single precision floating point numbers, about 16 decimal digits for double precision\\\\nfloating point numbers) and that floating point addition and multiplication are not\\\\nassociative, so the order of the operations affects the results.\\\\nBecause of this, PyTorch is not guaranteed\\\\nto produce bitwise identical results for floating point computations that are\\\\nmathematically identical. Similarly, bitwise identical results are not guaranteed across\\\\nPyTorch releases, individual commits, or different platforms. In particular, CPU and GPU\\\\nresults can be different even for bitwise-identical inputs and even after controlling for\\\\nthe sources of randomness.\\\\n\\\\nBatched computations or slice computations\\\\n------------------------------------------\\\\n\\\\nMany operations in PyTorch support batched computation, where the same operation is performed\\\\nfor the elements of the batches of inputs. An example of this is :meth:`torch.mm` and\\\\n:meth:`torch.bmm`. It is possible to implement batched computation as a loop over batch elements,\\\\nand apply the necessary math operations to the individual batch elements, for efficiency reasons\\\\nwe are not doing that, and typically perform computation for the whole batch. The mathematical\\\\nlibraries that we are calling, and PyTorch internal implementations of operations can produce\\\\nslightly different results in this case, compared to non-batched computations. In particular,\\\\nlet ``A`` and ``B`` be 3D tensors with the dimensions suitable for batched matrix multiplication.\\\\nThen ``(A@B)[0]`` (the first element of the batched result) is not guaranteed to be bitwise\\\\nidentical to ``A[0]@B[0]`` (the matrix product of the first elements of the input batches)\\\\neven though mathematically it's an identical computation.\\\\n\\\\nSimilarly, an operation applied to a tensor slice is not guaranteed to produce results that are\\\\nidentical to the slice of the result of the same operation applied to the full tensor. E.g. let\\\\n``A`` be a 2-dimensional tensor. ``A.sum(-1)[0]`` is not guaranteed to be bitwise equal to\\\\n``A[:,0].sum()``.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nExtremal values\\\\n---------------\\\\n\\\\nWhen inputs contain large values such that intermediate results may overflow the range of the\\\\nused datatype, the end result may overflow too, even though it is representable in the original\\\\ndatatype. E.g.:\\\\n\\\\n.. code:: python\\\\n\\\\n    import torch\\\\n    a=torch.tensor([1e20, 1e20]) # fp32 type by default\\\\n    a.norm() # produces tensor(inf)\\\\n    a.double().norm() # produces tensor(1.4142e+20, dtype=torch.float64), representable in fp32\\\\n\\\\n.. _Linear Algebra Stability:\\\\n\\\\nLinear algebra (``torch.linalg``)\\\\n---------------------------------\\\\n\\\\nNon-finite values\\\\n\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nThe external libraries (backends) that ``torch.linalg`` uses provide no guarantees on their behaviour\\\\nwhen the inputs have non-finite values like ``inf`` or ``NaN``. As such, neither does PyTorch.\\\\nThe operations may return a tensor with non-finite values, or raise an exception, or even segfault.\\\\n\\\\nConsider using :func:`torch.isfinite` before calling these functions to detect this situation.\\\\n\\\\nExtremal values in linalg\\\\n\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nFunctions within ``torch.linalg`` have more `Extremal Values`_ than other PyTorch functions.\\\\n\\\\n:ref:`linalg solvers` and :ref:`linalg inverses` assume that the input matrix ``A`` is invertible. If it is close to\\\\nbeing non-invertible (for example, if it has a very small singular value), then these algorithms may silently return\\\\nincorrect results. These matrices are said to be `ill-conditioned <https://nhigham.com/2020/03/19/what-is-a-condition-number/>`_.\\\\nIf provided with ill-conditioned inputs, the result of these functions they may vary when using the same inputs on different\\\\ndevices or when using different backends via the keyword ``driver``.\\\\n\\\\nSpectral operations like ``svd``, ``eig``, and ``eigh`` may also return incorrect results (and their gradients may be infinite)\\\\nwhen their inputs have singular values that are close to each other. This is because the algorithms used to compute these decompositions\\\\nstruggle to converge for these inputs.\\\\n\\\\nRunning the computation in ``float64`` (as NumPy does by default) often helps, but it does not solve these issues in all cases.\\\\nAnalyzing the spectrum of the inputs via :func:`torch.linalg.svdvals` or their condition number via :func:`torch.linalg.cond`\\\\nmay help to detect these issues.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nTensorFloat-32(TF32) on Nvidia Ampere (and later) devices\\\\n---------------------------------------------------------\\\\n\\\\nOn Ampere (and later) Nvidia GPUs, PyTorch can use TensorFloat32 (TF32) to speed up mathematically intensive operations, in particular matrix multiplications and convolutions.\\\\nWhen an operation is performed using TF32 tensor cores, only the first 10 bits of the input mantissa are read.\\\\nThis may reduce accuracy and produce surprising results (e.g., multiplying a matrix by the identity matrix may produce results that are different from the input).\\\\nBy default, TF32 tensor cores are disabled for matrix multiplications and enabled for convolutions, although most neural network workloads have the same convergence behavior when using TF32 as they have with fp32.\\\\nWe recommend enabling TF32 tensor cores for matrix multiplications with ``torch.backends.cuda.matmul.fp32_precision = \\\\\\\"tf32\\\\\\\"`` (```torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True`` is going to be deprecated) if your network does not need full float32 precision.\\\\nIf your network needs full float32 precision for both matrix multiplications and convolutions, then TF32 tensor cores can also be disabled for convolutions with ``torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision = \\\\\\\"ieee\\\\\\\"`` (``torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = False`` is going to be deprecated).\\\\n\\\\nFor more information see :ref:`TensorFloat32<tf32_on_ampere>`.\\\\n\\\\nReduced Precision Reduction for FP16 and BF16 GEMMs\\\\n----------------------------------------------------\\\\nHalf-precision GEMM operations are typically done with intermediate accumulations (reduction) in single-precision for numerical accuracy and improved resilience to overflow. For performance, certain GPU architectures, especially more recent ones, allow a few truncations of the intermediate accumulation results to the reduced precision (e.g., half-precision). This change is often benign from the perspective of model convergence, though it may lead to unexpected results (e.g., ``inf`` values when the final result should be be representable in half-precision).\\\\nIf reduced-precision reductions are problematic, they can be turned off with\\\\n``torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_fp16_reduced_precision_reduction = False``\\\\n\\\\nA similar flag exists for BF16 GEMM operations and is turned on by default. If BF16\\\\nreduced-precision reductions are problematic, they can be turned off with\\\\n``torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_bf16_reduced_precision_reduction = False``\\\\n\\\\nFor more information see :ref:`allow_fp16_reduced_precision_reduction<fp16reducedprecision>` and :ref:`allow_bf16_reduced_precision_reduction<bf16reducedprecision>`\\\\n\\\\nReduced Precision Reduction for FP16 and BF16 in Scaled Dot Product Attention (SDPA)\\\\n------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\\\nA naive SDPA math backend, when using FP16/BF16 inputs, can accumulate significant numerical errors due to the usage of low-precision intermediate buffers. To mitigate this issue, the default behavior now involves upcasting FP16/BF16 inputs to FP32. Computations are performed in FP32/TF32, and the final FP32 results are then downcasted back to FP16/BF16. This will improve numerical accuracy of the final output for the math backend with FP16/BF16 inputs, but increases memory usages and may cause the performance regressions in the math backend as computations shift from FP16/BF16 BMM to FP32/TF32 BMM/Matmul.\\\\n\\\\nFor scenarios where reduced-precision reductions are preferred for speed, they can be enabled with the following setting:\\\\n``torch.backends.cuda.allow_fp16_bf16_reduction_math_sdp(True)``\\\\n\\\\n.. _fp16_on_mi200:\\\\n\\\\nReduced Precision FP16 and BF16 GEMMs and Convolutions on AMD Instinct MI200 devices\\\\n------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\\\nOn AMD Instinct MI200 GPUs, the FP16 and BF16 V_DOT2 and MFMA matrix instructions flush input and output denormal values to zero. FP32 and FP64 MFMA matrix instructions do not flush input and output denormal values to zero. The affected instructions are only used by rocBLAS (GEMM) and MIOpen (convolution) kernels; all other PyTorch operations will not encounter this behavior. All other supported AMD GPUs will not encounter this behavior.\\\\n\\\\nrocBLAS and MIOpen provide alternate implementations for affected FP16 operations. Alternate implementations for BF16 operations are not provided; BF16 numbers have a larger dynamic range than FP16 numbers and are less likely to encounter denormal values. For the FP16 alternate implementations, FP16 input values are cast to an intermediate BF16 value and then cast back to FP16 output after the accumulate FP32 operations. In this way, the input and output types are unchanged.\\\\n\\\\nWhen training using FP16 precision, some models may fail to converge with FP16 denorms flushed to zero. Denormal values more frequently occur in the backward pass of training during gradient calculation. PyTorch by default will use the rocBLAS and MIOpen alternate implementations during the backward pass. The default behavior can be overridden using environment variables, ROCBLAS_INTERNAL_FP16_ALT_IMPL and MIOPEN_DEBUG_CONVOLUTION_ATTRIB_FP16_ALT_IMPL. The behavior of these environment variables is as follows:\\\\n\\\\n+---------------+-----------+-----------+\\\\n|               | forward   | backward  |\\\\n+===============+===========+===========+\\\\n| Env unset     | original  | alternate |\\\\n+---------------+-----------+-----------+\\\\n| Env set to 1  | alternate | alternate |\\\\n+---------------+-----------+-----------+\\\\n| Env set to 0  | original  | original  |\\\\n+---------------+-----------+-----------+\\\\n\\\\nThe following is the list of operations where rocBLAS may be used:\\\\n\\\\n* torch.addbmm\\\\n* torch.addmm\\\\n* torch.baddbmm\\\\n* torch.bmm\\\\n* torch.mm\\\\n* torch.nn.GRUCell\\\\n* torch.nn.LSTMCell\\\\n* torch.nn.Linear\\\\n* torch.sparse.addmm\\\\n* the following torch._C._ConvBackend implementations:\\\\n\\\\n  * slowNd\\\\n  * slowNd_transposed\\\\n  * slowNd_dilated\\\\n  * slowNd_dilated_transposed\\\\n\\\\nThe following is the list of operations where MIOpen may be used:\\\\n\\\\n* torch.nn.Conv[Transpose]Nd\\\\n* the following torch._C._ConvBackend implementations:\\\\n\\\\n  * ConvBackend::Miopen\\\\n  * ConvBackend::MiopenDepthwise\\\\n  * ConvBackend::MiopenTranspose\\\\n\\\", \\\"excerpt_ranges\\\": [[0, 10998]], \\\"range_unit\\\": \\\"zero-based half-open characters in extracted text\\\", \\\"extracted_characters\\\": 10998, \\\"selected_characters\\\": 10998, \\\"extraction\\\": \\\"UTF-8 text\\\", \\\"selection_reason\\\": \\\"full extracted text fits allocation\\\"}, {\\\"path\\\": \\\"references/S-TORCH-REPRO/fulltext.txt\\\", \\\"sha256\\\": \\\"4f6b1deb38f7f174a2e340674680aaa0484e02a1d18cccd1bb94618df512cc2a\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"source_original\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"\\\\n===== docs/source/notes/randomness.rst =====\\\\n.. _reproducibility:\\\\n\\\\nReproducibility\\\\n===============\\\\n\\\\nCompletely reproducible results are not guaranteed across PyTorch releases,\\\\nindividual commits, or different platforms. Furthermore, results may not be\\\\nreproducible between CPU and GPU executions, even when using identical seeds.\\\\n\\\\nHowever, there are some steps you can take to limit the number of sources of\\\\nnondeterministic behavior for a specific platform, device, and PyTorch release.\\\\nFirst, you can control sources of randomness that can cause multiple executions\\\\nof your application to behave differently. Second, you can configure PyTorch\\\\nto avoid using nondeterministic algorithms for some operations, so that multiple\\\\ncalls to those operations, given the same inputs, will produce the same result.\\\\n\\\\n.. warning::\\\\n\\\\n    Deterministic operations are often slower than nondeterministic operations, so\\\\n    single-run performance may decrease for your model. However, determinism may\\\\n    save time in development by facilitating experimentation, debugging, and\\\\n    regression testing.\\\\n\\\\nControlling sources of randomness\\\\n.................................\\\\n\\\\nPyTorch random number generator\\\\n-------------------------------\\\\nYou can use :meth:`torch.manual_seed()` to seed the RNG for all devices (both\\\\nCPU and CUDA)::\\\\n\\\\n    import torch\\\\n    torch.manual_seed(0)\\\\n\\\\nSome PyTorch operations may use random numbers internally.\\\\n:meth:`torch.svd_lowrank()` does this, for instance. Consequently, calling it\\\\nmultiple times back-to-back with the same input arguments may give different\\\\nresults. However, as long as :meth:`torch.manual_seed()` is set to a constant\\\\nat the beginning of an application and all other sources of nondeterminism have\\\\nbeen eliminated, the same series of random numbers will be generated each time\\\\nthe application is run in the same environment.\\\\n\\\\nIt is also possible to obtain identical results from an operation that uses\\\\nrandom numbers by setting :meth:`torch.manual_seed()` to the same value between\\\\nsubsequent calls.\\\\n\\\\nPython\\\\n------\\\\n\\\\nFor custom operators, you might need to set python seed as well::\\\\n\\\\n    import random\\\\n    random.seed(0)\\\\n\\\\nRandom number generators in other libraries\\\\n-------------------------------------------\\\\nIf you or any of the libraries you are using rely on NumPy, you can seed the global\\\\nNumPy RNG with::\\\\n\\\\n    import numpy as np\\\\n    np.random.seed(0)\\\\n\\\\nHowever, some applications and libraries may use NumPy Random Generator objects,\\\\nnot the global RNG\\\\n(`<https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/random/generator.html>`_), and those will\\\\nneed to be seeded consistently as well.\\\\n\\\\nIf you are using any other libraries that use random number generators, refer to\\\\nthe documentation for those libraries to see how to set consistent seeds for them.\\\\n\\\\nCUDA convolution benchmarking\\\\n-----------------------------\\\\nThe cuDNN library, used by CUDA convolution operations, can be a source of nondeterminism\\\\nacross multiple executions of an application. When a cuDNN convolution is called with a\\\\nnew set of size parameters, an optional feature can run multiple convolution algorithms,\\\\nbenchmarking them to find the fastest one. Then, the fastest algorithm will be used\\\\nconsistently during the rest of the process for the corresponding set of size parameters.\\\\nDue to benchmarking noise and different hardware, the benchmark may select different\\\\nalgorithms on subsequent runs, even on the same machine.\\\\n\\\\nDisabling the benchmarking feature with :code:`torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False`\\\\ncauses cuDNN to deterministically select an algorithm, possibly at the cost of reduced\\\\nperformance.\\\\n\\\\nHowever, if you do not need reproducibility across multiple executions of your application,\\\\nthen performance might improve if the benchmarking feature is enabled with\\\\n:code:`torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = True`.\\\\n\\\\nNote that this setting is different from the :code:`torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic`\\\\nsetting discussed below.\\\\n\\\\nAvoiding nondeterministic algorithms\\\\n....................................\\\\n:meth:`torch.use_deterministic_algorithms` lets you configure PyTorch to use\\\\ndeterministic algorithms instead of nondeterministic ones where available, and\\\\nto throw an error if an operation is known to be nondeterministic (and without\\\\na deterministic alternative).\\\\n\\\\nPlease check the documentation for :meth:`torch.use_deterministic_algorithms()`\\\\nfor a full list of affected operations. If an operation does not act correctly\\\\naccording to the documentation, or if you need a deterministic implementation\\\\nof an operation that does not have one, please submit an issue:\\\\n`<https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=label:%22module:%20determinism%22>`_\\\\n\\\\nFor example, running the nondeterministic CUDA implementation of :meth:`torch.Tensor.index_add_`\\\\nwill throw an error::\\\\n\\\\n    >>> import torch\\\\n    >>> torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)\\\\n    >>> torch.randn(2, 2).cuda().index_add_(0, torch.tensor([0, 1]), torch.randn(2, 2))\\\\n    Traceback (most recent call last):\\\\n    File \\\\\\\"<stdin>\\\\\\\", line 1, in <module>\\\\n    RuntimeError: index_add_cuda_ does not have a deterministic implementation, but you set\\\\n    'torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)'. ...\\\\n\\\\nWhen :meth:`torch.bmm` is called with sparse-dense CUDA tensors it typically uses a\\\\nnondeterministic algorithm, but when the deterministic flag is turned on, its alternate\\\\ndeterministic implementation will be used::\\\\n\\\\n    >>> import torch\\\\n    >>> torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)\\\\n    >>> torch.bmm(torch.randn(2, 2, 2).to_sparse().cuda(), torch.randn(2, 2, 2).cuda())\\\\n    tensor([[[ 1.1900, -2.3409],\\\\n             [ 0.4796,  0.8003]],\\\\n            [[ 0.1509,  1.8027],\\\\n             [ 0.0333, -1.1444]]], device='cuda:0')\\\\n\\\\nCUDA convolution determinism\\\\n----------------------------\\\\nWhile disabling CUDA convolution benchmarking (discussed above) ensures that\\\\nCUDA selects the same algorithm each time an application is run, that algorithm\\\\nitself may be nondeterministic, unless either\\\\n:code:`torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` or\\\\n:code:`torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True` is set. The latter setting\\\\ncontrols only this behavior, unlike :meth:`torch.use_deterministic_algorithms`\\\\nwhich will make other PyTorch operations behave deterministically, too.\\\\n\\\\nCUDA RNN and LSTM\\\\n-----------------\\\\nIn some versions of CUDA, RNNs and LSTM networks may have non-deterministic behavior.\\\\nSee :meth:`torch.nn.RNN` and :meth:`torch.nn.LSTM` for details and workarounds.\\\\n\\\\nFilling uninitialized memory\\\\n----------------------------\\\\nOperations like :meth:`torch.empty` and :meth:`torch.Tensor.resize_` can return\\\\ntensors with uninitialized memory that contain undefined values. Using such a\\\\ntensor as an input to another operation is invalid if determinism is required,\\\\nbecause the output will be nondeterministic. But there is nothing to actually\\\\nprevent such invalid code from being run. So for safety,\\\\n:attr:`torch.utils.deterministic.fill_uninitialized_memory` is set to ``True``\\\\nby default, which will fill the uninitialized memory with a known value if\\\\n:code:`torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` is set. This will prevent the\\\\npossibility of this kind of nondeterministic behavior.\\\\n\\\\nHowever, filling uninitialized memory is detrimental to performance. So if your\\\\nprogram is valid and does not use uninitialized memory as the input to an\\\\noperation, then this setting can be turned off for better performance.\\\\n\\\\nDataLoader\\\\n..........\\\\n\\\\nDataLoader will reseed workers following :ref:`data-loading-randomness` algorithm.\\\\nUse :meth:`worker_init_fn` and `generator` to preserve reproducibility::\\\\n\\\\n    def seed_worker(worker_id):\\\\n        worker_seed = torch.initial_seed() % 2**32\\\\n        numpy.random.seed(worker_seed)\\\\n        random.seed(worker_seed)\\\\n\\\\n    g = torch.Generator()\\\\n    g.manual_seed(0)\\\\n\\\\n    DataLoader(\\\\n        train_dataset,\\\\n        batch_size=batch_size,\\\\n        num_workers=num_workers,\\\\n        worker_init_fn=seed_worker,\\\\n        generator=g,\\\\n    )\\\\n\\\", \\\"excerpt_ranges\\\": [[0, 7936]], \\\"range_unit\\\": \\\"zero-based half-open characters in extracted text\\\", \\\"extracted_characters\\\": 7936, \\\"selected_characters\\\": 7936, \\\"extraction\\\": \\\"UTF-8 text\\\", \\\"selection_reason\\\": \\\"full extracted text fits allocation\\\"}, {\\\"path\\\": \\\"references/S-HF-CACHE/fulltext.txt\\\", \\\"sha256\\\": \\\"373837b8ac246d43867eb21de168cc59e5e6e78f5f3b9c27bee54740c4a635b4\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"source_original\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"\\\\n===== docs/source/en/cache_explanation.md =====\\\\n<!--Copyright 2024 The HuggingFace Team. This would be slow and inefficient, right?\\\\n\\\\nYou can extend this analogy to transformer models. Autoregressive model generation can be slow because it makes a prediction one token at a time. Each new prediction is dependent on all the previous context.\\\\n\\\\nTo predict the 1000th token, the model requires information from the previous 999 tokens. The information is represented as matrix multiplications across the token representations.\\\\n\\\\nTo predict the 1001th token, you need the same information from the previous 999 tokens in addition to any information from the 1000th token. This is a lot of matrix multiplications a model has to compute over and over for each token!\\\\n\\\\nA key-value (KV) cache eliminates this inefficiency by storing kv pairs derived from the attention layers of previously processed tokens. The stored kv pairs are retrieved from the cache and reused for subsequent tokens, avoiding the need to recompute.\\\\n\\\\n> [!WARNING]\\\\n> Caching should only be used for **inference**. It may cause unexpected errors if it's enabled during training.\\\\n\\\\nTo better understand how and why caching works, let's take a closer look at the structure of the attention matrices.\\\\n\\\\n## Attention matrices\\\\n\\\\nThe **scaled dot-product attention** is calculated as shown below for a batch of size `b`, number of attention heads `h`, sequence length so far `T`, and dimension per attention head `d_head`.\\\\n\\\\n$$\\\\n\\\\\\\\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \\\\\\\\text{softmax}\\\\\\\\left( \\\\\\\\frac{Q K^\\\\\\\\top}{\\\\\\\\sqrt{d_{\\\\\\\\text{head}}}} \\\\\\\\times \\\\\\\\text{mask} \\\\\\\\right) V\\\\n$$\\\\n\\\\nThe query (`Q`), key (`K`), and value (`V`) matrices are projections from the input embeddings of shape `(b, h, T, d_head)`.\\\\n\\\\nFor causal attention, the mask prevents the model from attending to future tokens. Once a token is processed, its representation never changes with respect to future tokens, which means $ K_{\\\\\\\\text{past}} $ and $ V_{\\\\\\\\text{past}} $ can be cached and reused to compute the last token's representation.\\\\n\\\\n$$\\\\n\\\\\\\\text{Attention}(q_t, [\\\\\\\\underbrace{k_1, k_2, \\\\\\\\dots, k_{t-1}}_{\\\\\\\\text{cached}}, k_{t}], [\\\\\\\\underbrace{v_1, v_2, \\\\\\\\dots, v_{t-1}}_{\\\\\\\\text{cached}}, v_{t}])\\\\n$$\\\\n\\\\nAt inference time, you only need the last token's query to compute the representation $ x_t $ that predicts the next token $ t+1 $. At each step, the new key and value vectors are **stored** in the cache and **appended** to the past keys and values.\\\\n\\\\n$$\\\\nK_{\\\\\\\\text{cache}} \\\\\\\\leftarrow \\\\\\\\text{concat}(K_{\\\\\\\\text{past}}, k_t), \\\\\\\\quad V_{\\\\\\\\text{cache}} \\\\\\\\leftarrow \\\\\\\\text{concat}(V_{\\\\\\\\text{past}}, v_t)\\\\n$$\\\\n\\\\nAttention is calculated independently in each layer of the model, and caching is done on a per-layer basis.\\\\n\\\\nRefer to the table below to compare how caching improves efficiency.\\\\n\\\\n| without caching | with caching |\\\\n|---|---|\\\\n| for each step, recompute all previous `K` and `V`  | for each step, only compute current `K` and `V` |\\\\n| attention cost per step is **quadratic** with sequence length | attention cost per step is **linear** with sequence length (memory grows linearly, but compute/token remains low) |\\\\n\\\\n## Cache class\\\\n\\\\nA basic KV cache interface takes a key and value tensor for the current token and returns the updated `K` and `V` tensors. This is internally managed by a model's `forward` method.\\\\n\\\\n```py\\\\nnew_K, new_V = cache.update(k_t, v_t, layer_idx)\\\\nattn_output = attn_layer_idx_fn(q_t, new_K, new_V)\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nWhen you use Transformers' [`Cache`] class, the self-attention module performs several critical steps to integrate past and present information.\\\\n\\\\n1. The attention module concatenates current kv pairs with past kv pairs stored in the cache. This creates attentions weights with the shape `(new_tokens_length, past_kv_length + new_tokens_length)`. The current and past kv pairs are essentially combined to compute the attention scores, ensuring a model is aware of previous context and the current input.\\\\n\\\\n2. When the `forward` method is called iteratively, it's crucial that the attention mask shape matches the combined length of the past and current kv pairs. The attention mask should have the shape `(batch_size, past_kv_length + new_tokens_length)`. This is typically handled internally in [`~GenerationMixin.generate`], but if you want to implement your own generation loop with [`Cache`], keep this in mind! The attention mask should hold the past and current token values.\\\\n\\\\n## Cache storage implementation\\\\n\\\\nCaches are structured as a list of layers, where each layer contains a key and value cache. The key and value caches are tensors with the shape `[batch_size, num_heads, seq_len, head_dim]`.\\\\n\\\\nLayers can be of different types (e.g. `DynamicLayer`, `StaticLayer`, `StaticSlidingWindowLayer`), which mostly changes how sequence length is handled and how the cache is updated.\\\\n\\\\nThe simplest is a `DynamicLayer` that grows as more tokens are processed. The sequence length dimension (`seq_len`) increases with each new token:\\\\n\\\\n```py\\\\ncache.layers[idx].keys = torch.cat([cache.layers[idx].keys, key_states], dim=-2)\\\\ncache.layers[idx].values = torch.cat([cache.layers[idx].values, value_states], dim=-2)\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nOther layer types like `StaticLayer` and `StaticSlidingWindowLayer` have a fixed sequence length that is set when the cache is created. This makes them compatible with `torch.compile`. In the case of `StaticSlidingWindowLayer`, existing tokens are shifted out of the cache when a new token is added.\\\\n\\\\nThe example below demonstrates how to create a generation loop with [`DynamicCache`]. As discussed, the attention mask is a concatenation of past and current token values.\\\\n\\\\n```py\\\\nimport torch\\\\nfrom transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM, DynamicCache\\\\nfrom accelerate import Accelerator\\\\n\\\\ndevice = Accelerator().device\\\\n\\\\nmodel_id = \\\\\\\"meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf\\\\\\\"\\\\nmodel = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map=device)\\\\ntokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)\\\\n\\\\npast_key_values = DynamicCache(config=model.config)\\\\nmessages = [{\\\\\\\"role\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"user\\\\\\\", \\\\\\\"content\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"Hello, what's your name.\\\\\\\"}]\\\\ninputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors=\\\\\\\"pt\\\\\\\", return_dict=True).to(model.device)\\\\n\\\\ngenerated_ids = inputs.input_ids\\\\nmax_new_tokens = 10\\\\n\\\\nfor _ in range(max_new_tokens):\\\\n    outputs = model(**inputs, past_key_values=past_key_values, use_cache=True)\\\\n    # Greedily sample one next token\\\\n    next_token_ids = outputs.logits[:, -1:].argmax(-1)\\\\n    generated_ids = torch.cat([generated_ids, next_token_ids], dim=-1)\\\\n    # Prepare inputs for the next generation step by leaving unprocessed tokens, in our case we have only one new token\\\\n    # and expanding attn mask for the new token, as explained above\\\\n    attention_mask = inputs[\\\\\\\"attention_mask\\\\\\\"]\\\\n    attention_mask = torch.cat([attention_mask, attention_mask.new_ones((attention_mask.shape[0], 1))], dim=-1)\\\\n    inputs = {\\\\\\\"input_ids\\\\\\\": next_token_ids, \\\\\\\"attention_mask\\\\\\\": attention_mask}\\\\n\\\\nprint(tokenizer.batch_decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)[0])\\\\n\\\\\\\"[INST] Hello, what's your name. [/INST]  Hello! My name is LLaMA,\\\\\\\"\\\\n```\\\\n\\\", \\\"excerpt_ranges\\\": [[0, 7977]], \\\"range_unit\\\": \\\"zero-based half-open characters in extracted text\\\", \\\"extracted_characters\\\": 7977, \\\"selected_characters\\\": 7977, \\\"extraction\\\": \\\"UTF-8 text\\\", \\\"selection_reason\\\": \\\"full extracted text fits allocation\\\"}, {\\\"path\\\": \\\"references/S-ASGI/fulltext.txt\\\", \\\"sha256\\\": \\\"ba273c91f3e7b8c32f863e8b57145798c3b5c9275073f758a41e1cb0a6f5bee3\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"source_original\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"\\\\n===== specs/www.rst =====\\\\n====================================\\\\nHTTP & WebSocket ASGI Message Format\\\\n====================================\\\\n\\\\n**Version**: 2.5 (2024-06-05)\\\\n\\\\nThe HTTP+WebSocket ASGI sub-specification outlines how to transport HTTP/1.1,\\\\nHTTP/2 and WebSocket connections within ASGI.\\\\n\\\\nIt is deliberately intended and designed to be a superset of the WSGI format\\\\nand specifies how to translate between the two for the set of requests that\\\\nare able to be handled by WSGI.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nSpec Versions\\\\n-------------\\\\n\\\\nThis spec has had the following versions:\\\\n\\\\n* ``2.0``: The first version of the spec, released with ASGI 2.0\\\\n* ``2.1``: Added the ``headers`` key to the WebSocket Accept response\\\\n* ``2.2``: Allow ``None`` in the second item of ``server`` scope value.\\\\n* ``2.3``: Added the ``reason`` key to the WebSocket close event.\\\\n* ``2.4``: Calling ``send()`` on a closed connection should raise an error\\\\n* ``2.5``: Added the ``reason`` key to the WebSocket disconnect event.\\\\n\\\\nSpec versions let you understand what the server you are using understands. If\\\\na server tells you it only supports version ``2.0`` of this spec, then\\\\nsending ``headers`` with a WebSocket Accept message is an error, for example.\\\\n\\\\nThey are separate from the HTTP version or the ASGI version.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nHTTP\\\\n----\\\\n\\\\nThe HTTP format covers HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, as the changes in\\\\nHTTP/2 are largely on the transport level. A protocol server should give\\\\ndifferent scopes to different requests on the same HTTP/2 connection, and\\\\ncorrectly multiplex the responses back to the same stream in which they came.\\\\nThe HTTP version is available as a string in the scope.\\\\n\\\\nMultiple header fields with the same name are complex in HTTP. RFC 7230\\\\nstates that for any header field that can appear multiple times, it is exactly\\\\nequivalent to sending that header field only once with all the values joined by\\\\ncommas.\\\\n\\\\nHowever, for HTTP cookies (``Cookie`` and ``Set-Cookie``) the allowed behaviour\\\\ndoes not follow the above rule, and also varies slightly based on the HTTP\\\\nprotocol version:\\\\n\\\\n* For the ``Set-Cookie`` header in HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP2.0, it may appear\\\\n  repeatedly, but cannot be concatenated by commas (or anything else) into a\\\\n  single header field.\\\\n\\\\n* For the ``Cookie`` header, in HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1, RFC 7230 and RFC 6265\\\\n  make it clear that the ``Cookie`` header must only be sent once by a\\\\n  user-agent, and must be concatenated into a single octet string using the\\\\n  two-octet delimiter of 0x3b, 0x20 (the ASCII string \\\\\\\"; \\\\\\\"). However in HTTP/2,\\\\n  RFC 9113 states that ``Cookie`` headers MAY appear repeatedly, OR be\\\\n  concatenated using the two-octet delimiter of 0x3b, 0x20\\\\n  (the ASCII string \\\\\\\"; \\\\\\\").\\\\n\\\\nThe ASGI design decision is to transport both request and response headers as\\\\nlists of 2-element ``[name, value]`` lists and preserve headers exactly as they\\\\nwere provided.\\\\n\\\\nFor ASGI applications that support HTTP/2, care should be taken to handle the\\\\nspecial case for ``Cookie`` noted above.\\\\n\\\\nThe HTTP protocol should be signified to ASGI applications with a ``type``\\\\nvalue of ``http``.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nHTTP Connection Scope\\\\n'''''''''''''''''''''\\\\n\\\\nHTTP connections have a single-request *connection scope* - that is, your\\\\napplication will be called at the start of the request, and will last until\\\\nthe end of that specific request, even if the underlying socket is still open\\\\nand serving multiple requests.\\\\n\\\\nIf you hold a response open for long-polling or similar, the *connection scope*\\\\nwill persist until the response closes from either the client or server side.\\\\n\\\\nThe *connection scope* information passed in ``scope`` contains:\\\\n\\\\n* ``type`` (*Unicode string*) -- ``\\\\\\\"http\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``asgi[\\\\\\\"version\\\\\\\"]`` (*Unicode string*) -- Version of the ASGI spec.\\\\n\\\\n* ``asgi[\\\\\\\"spec_version\\\\\\\"]`` (*Unicode string*) -- Version of the ASGI\\\\n  HTTP spec this server understands; for example: ``\\\\\\\"2.0\\\\\\\"``, ``\\\\\\\"2.1\\\\\\\"``, ``\\\\\\\"2.2\\\\\\\"``,\\\\n  etc. Optional; if missing assume ``\\\\\\\"2.0\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``http_version`` (*Unicode string*) -- One of ``\\\\\\\"1.0\\\\\\\"``, ``\\\\\\\"1.1\\\\\\\"`` or ``\\\\\\\"2\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``method`` (*Unicode string*) -- The HTTP method name, uppercased.\\\\n\\\\n* ``scheme`` (*Unicode string*) -- URL scheme portion (likely ``\\\\\\\"http\\\\\\\"`` or\\\\n  ``\\\\\\\"https\\\\\\\"``). Optional (but must not be empty); default is ``\\\\\\\"http\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``path`` (*Unicode string*) -- HTTP request target excluding any query\\\\n  string, with percent-encoded sequences and UTF-8 byte sequences\\\\n  decoded into characters.\\\\n\\\\n* ``raw_path`` (*byte string*) -- The original HTTP path component,\\\\n  excluding any query string, unmodified from the bytes that were\\\\n  received by the web server. Some web server implementations may\\\\n  be unable to provide this. Optional; if missing defaults to ``None``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``query_string`` (*byte string*) -- URL portion after the ``?``,\\\\n  percent-encoded.\\\\n\\\\n* ``root_path`` (*Unicode string*) -- The root path this application\\\\n  is mounted at; same as ``SCRIPT_NAME`` in WSGI. Optional; if missing\\\\n  defaults to ``\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``headers`` (*Iterable[[byte string, byte string]]*) -- An iterable of\\\\n  ``[name, value]`` two-item iterables, where ``name`` is the header name, and\\\\n  ``value`` is the header value. Order of header values must be preserved from\\\\n  the original HTTP request; order of header names is not important. Duplicates\\\\n  are possible and must be preserved in the message as received. Header names\\\\n  should be lowercased, but it is not required; servers should preserve header case\\\\n  on a best-effort basis. Pseudo headers (present in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3) must be\\\\n  removed; if ``:authority`` is present its value must be added to the start of\\\\n  the iterable with ``host`` as the header name or replace any existing host\\\\n  header already present.\\\\n\\\\n* ``client`` (*Iterable[Unicode string, int]*) -- A two-item iterable\\\\n  of ``[host, port]``, where ``host`` is the remote host's IPv4 or\\\\n  IPv6 address, and ``port`` is the remote port as an\\\\n  integer. Optional; if missing defaults to ``None``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``server`` (*Iterable[Unicode string, Optional[int]]*) -- Either a\\\\n  two-item iterable of ``[host, port]``, where ``host`` is the\\\\n  listening address for this server, and ``port`` is the integer\\\\n  listening port, or ``[path, None]`` where ``path`` is that of the\\\\n  unix socket. Optional; if missing defaults to ``None``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``state`` Optional(*dict[Unicode string, Any]*) -- A copy of the\\\\n  namespace passed into the lifespan corresponding to this request. (See :doc:`lifespan`).\\\\n  Optional; if missing the server does not support this feature.\\\\n\\\\nServers are responsible for handling inbound and outbound chunked transfer\\\\nencodings. A request with a ``chunked`` encoded body should be automatically\\\\nde-chunked by the server and presented to the application as plain body bytes;\\\\na response that is given to the server with no ``Content-Length`` may be chunked\\\\nas the server sees fit.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nRequest - ``receive`` event\\\\n'''''''''''''''''''''''''''\\\\n\\\\nSent to the application to indicate an incoming request. Most of the request\\\\ninformation is in the connection ``scope``; the body message serves as a way to\\\\nstream large incoming HTTP bodies in chunks, and as a trigger to actually run\\\\nrequest code (as you should not trigger on a connection opening alone).\\\\n\\\\nNote that if the request is being sent using ``Transfer-Encoding: chunked``,\\\\nthe server is responsible for handling this encoding. The ``http.request``\\\\nmessages should contain just the decoded contents of each chunk.\\\\n\\\\nKeys:\\\\n\\\\n* ``type`` (*Unicode string*) -- ``\\\\\\\"http.request\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``body`` (*byte string*) -- Body of the request. Optional; if\\\\n  missing defaults to ``b\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"``. If ``more_body`` is set, treat as start\\\\n  of body and concatenate on further chunks.\\\\n\\\\n* ``more_body`` (*bool*) -- Signifies if there is additional content\\\\n  to come (as part of a Request message). If ``True``, the consuming\\\\n  application should wait until it gets a chunk with this set to\\\\n  ``False``. If ``False``, the request is complete and should be\\\\n  processed. Optional; if missing defaults to ``False``.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nResponse Start - ``send`` event\\\\n'''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''\\\\n\\\\nSent by the application to start sending a response to the client. Needs to be\\\\nfollowed by at least one response content message.\\\\n\\\\nProtocol servers *need not* flush the data generated by this event to the\\\\nsend buffer until the first *Response Body* event is processed.\\\\nThis may give them more leeway to replace the response with an error response\\\\nin case internal errors occur while handling the request.\\\\n\\\\nYou may send a ``Transfer-Encoding`` header in this message, but the server\\\\nmust ignore it. Servers handle ``Transfer-Encoding`` themselves, and may opt\\\\nto use ``Transfer-Encoding: chunked`` if the application presents a response\\\\nthat has no ``Content-Length`` set.\\\\n\\\\nNote that this is not the same as ``Content-Encoding``, which the application\\\\nstill controls, and which is the appropriate place to set ``gzip`` or other\\\\ncompression flags.\\\\n\\\\nKeys:\\\\n\\\\n* ``type`` (*Unicode string*) -- ``\\\\\\\"http.response.start\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``status`` (*int*) -- HTTP status code.\\\\n\\\\n* ``headers`` (*Iterable[[byte string, byte string]]*) -- An iterable\\\\n  of ``[name, value]`` two-item iterables, where ``name`` is the\\\\n  header name, and ``value`` is the header value. Order must be\\\\n  preserved in the HTTP response.  Header names must be\\\\n  lowercased. Optional; if missing defaults to an empty list. Pseudo\\\\n  headers (present in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3) must not be present.\\\\n\\\\n* ``trailers`` (*bool*) -- Signifies if the application will send\\\\n  trailers. If ``True``, the server must wait until it receives a\\\\n  ``\\\\\\\"http.response.trailers\\\\\\\"`` message after the *Response Body* event.\\\\n  Optional; if missing defaults to ``False``.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nResponse Body - ``send`` event\\\\n''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''\\\\n\\\\nContinues sending a response to the client. Protocol servers must\\\\nflush any data passed to them into the send buffer before returning from a\\\\nsend call. If ``more_body`` is set to ``False``, and the server is not\\\\nexpecting *Response Trailers* this will complete the response.\\\\n\\\\nKeys:\\\\n\\\\n* ``type`` (*Unicode string*) -- ``\\\\\\\"http.response.body\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``body`` (*byte string*) -- HTTP body content. Concatenated onto any\\\\n  previous ``body`` values sent in this connection scope. Optional; if\\\\n  missing defaults to ``b\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``more_body`` (*bool*) -- Signifies if there is additional content\\\\n  to come (as part of a *Response Body* message). If ``False``, and the\\\\n  server is not expecting *Response Trailers* response will be taken as\\\\n  complete and closed, and any further messages on the channel will be\\\\n  ignored. Optional; if missing defaults to ``False``.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nDisconnected Client - ``send`` exception\\\\n''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''\\\\n\\\\nIf ``send()`` is called on a closed connection the server should raise\\\\na server-specific subclass of ``OSError``. This is not guaranteed, however,\\\\nespecially on older ASGI server implementations (it was introduced in spec\\\\nversion 2.4).\\\\n\\\\nApplications may catch this exception and do cleanup work before\\\\nre-raising it or returning with no exception.\\\\n\\\\nServers must be prepared to catch this exception if they raised it and\\\\nshould not log it as an error in their server logs.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nDisconnect - ``receive`` event\\\\n''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''\\\\n\\\\nSent to the application if receive is called after a response has been\\\\nsent or after the HTTP connection has been closed. This is mainly useful\\\\nfor long-polling, where you may want to trigger cleanup code if the\\\\nconnection closes early.\\\\n\\\\nOnce you have received this event, you should expect future calls to ``send()``\\\\nto raise an exception, as described above. However, if you have highly\\\\nconcurrent code, you may find calls to ``send()`` erroring slightly before you\\\\nreceive this event.\\\\n\\\\nKeys:\\\\n\\\\n* ``type`` (*Unicode string*) -- ``\\\\\\\"http.disconnect\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nWebSocket\\\\n---------\\\\n\\\\nWebSockets share some HTTP details - they have a path and headers - but also\\\\nhave more state. Again, most of that state is in the ``scope``, which will live\\\\nas long as the socket does.\\\\n\\\\nWebSocket protocol servers should handle PING/PONG messages themselves, and\\\\nsend PING messages as necessary to ensure the connection is alive.\\\\n\\\\nWebSocket protocol servers should handle message fragmentation themselves,\\\\nand deliver complete messages to the application.\\\\n\\\\nThe WebSocket protocol should be signified to ASGI applications with\\\\na ``type`` value of ``websocket``.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nWebsocket Connection Scope\\\\n''''''''''''''''''''''''''\\\\n\\\\nWebSocket connections' scope lives as long as the socket itself - if the\\\\napplication dies the socket should be closed, and vice-versa.\\\\n\\\\nThe *connection scope* information passed in ``scope`` contains initial connection\\\\nmetadata (mostly from the HTTP request line and headers):\\\\n\\\\n* ``type`` (*Unicode string*) -- ``\\\\\\\"websocket\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``asgi[\\\\\\\"version\\\\\\\"]`` (*Unicode string*) -- The version of the ASGI spec.\\\\n\\\\n* ``asgi[\\\\\\\"spec_version\\\\\\\"]`` (*Unicode string*) -- Version of the ASGI\\\\n  HTTP spec this server understands; one of ``\\\\\\\"2.0\\\\\\\"``, ``\\\\\\\"2.1\\\\\\\"``, ``\\\\\\\"2.2\\\\\\\"`` or\\\\n  ``\\\\\\\"2.3\\\\\\\"``. Optional; if missing assume ``\\\\\\\"2.0\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``http_version`` (*Unicode string*) -- One of ``\\\\\\\"1.1\\\\\\\"`` or\\\\n  ``\\\\\\\"2\\\\\\\"``. Optional; if missing default is ``\\\\\\\"1.1\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``scheme`` (*Unicode string*) -- URL scheme portion (likely ``\\\\\\\"ws\\\\\\\"`` or\\\\n  ``\\\\\\\"wss\\\\\\\"``). Optional (but must not be empty); default is ``\\\\\\\"ws\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``path`` (*Unicode string*) -- HTTP request target excluding any query\\\\n  string, with percent-encoded sequences and UTF-8 byte sequences\\\\n  decoded into characters.\\\\n\\\\n* ``raw_path`` (*byte string*) -- The original HTTP path component,\\\\n  excluding any query string, unmodified from the bytes that were\\\\n  received by the web server. Some web server implementations may\\\\n  be unable to provide this. Optional; if missing defaults to ``None``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``query_string`` (*byte string*) -- URL portion after the\\\\n  ``?``. Optional; if missing or ``None`` default is empty string.\\\\n\\\\n* ``root_path`` (*Unicode string*) -- The root path this application is\\\\n  mounted at; same as ``SCRIPT_NAME`` in WSGI. Optional; if missing\\\\n  defaults to empty string.\\\\n\\\\n* ``headers`` (*Iterable[[byte string, byte string]]*) -- An iterable of\\\\n  ``[name, value]`` two-item iterables, where ``name`` is the header name and\\\\n  ``value`` is the header value. Order should be preserved from the original\\\\n  HTTP request; duplicates are possible and must be preserved in the message\\\\n  as received. Header names should be lowercased, but it is not required;\\\\n  servers should preserve header case on a best-effort basis.\\\\n  Pseudo headers (present in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3) must be removed;\\\\n  if ``:authority`` is present its value must be added to the\\\\n  start of the iterable with ``host`` as the header name\\\\n  or replace any existing host header already present.\\\\n\\\\n* ``client`` (*Iterable[Unicode string, int]*) -- A two-item iterable\\\\n  of ``[host, port]``, where ``host`` is the remote host's IPv4 or\\\\n  IPv6 address, and ``port`` is the remote port. Optional; if missing\\\\n  defaults to ``None``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``server`` (*Iterable[Unicode string, Optional[int]]*) -- Either a\\\\n  two-item iterable of ``[host, port]``, where ``host`` is the\\\\n  listening address for this server, and ``port`` is the integer\\\\n  listening port, or ``[path, None]`` where ``path`` is that of the\\\\n  unix socket. Optional; if missing defaults to ``None``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``subprotocols`` (*Iterable[Unicode string]*) -- Subprotocols the\\\\n  client advertised. Optional; if missing defaults to empty list.\\\\n\\\\n* ``state`` Optional(*dict[Unicode string, Any]*) -- A copy of the\\\\n  namespace passed into the lifespan corresponding to this request. (See :doc:`lifespan`).\\\\n  Optional; if missing the server does not support this feature.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nConnect - ``receive`` event\\\\n'''''''''''''''''''''''''''\\\\n\\\\nSent to the application when the client initially opens a connection and is about\\\\nto finish the WebSocket handshake.\\\\n\\\\nThis message must be responded to with either an *Accept* message\\\\nor a *Close* message before the socket will pass ``websocket.receive``\\\\nmessages. The protocol server must send this message\\\\nduring the handshake phase of the WebSocket and not complete the handshake\\\\nuntil it gets a reply, returning HTTP status code ``403`` if the connection is\\\\ndenied.\\\\n\\\\nKeys:\\\\n\\\\n* ``type`` (*Unicode string*) -- ``\\\\\\\"websocket.connect\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nAccept - ``send`` event\\\\n'''''''''''''''''''''''\\\\n\\\\nSent by the application when it wishes to accept an incoming connection.\\\\n\\\\n* ``type`` (*Unicode string*) -- ``\\\\\\\"websocket.accept\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``subprotocol`` (*Unicode string*) -- The subprotocol the server\\\\n  wishes to accept. Optional; if missing defaults to ``None``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``headers`` (*Iterable[[byte string, byte string]]*) -- An iterable\\\\n  of ``[name, value]`` two-item iterables, where ``name`` is the\\\\n  header name, and ``value`` is the header value. Order must be\\\\n  preserved in the HTTP response.  Header names must be\\\\n  lowercased. Must not include a header named\\\\n  ``sec-websocket-protocol``; use the ``subprotocol`` key\\\\n  instead. Optional; if missing defaults to an empty list. *Added in\\\\n  spec version 2.1*. Pseudo headers (present in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3)\\\\n  must not be present.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nReceive - ``receive`` event\\\\n'''''''''''''''''''''''''''\\\\n\\\\nSent to the application when a data message is received from the client.\\\\n\\\\nKeys:\\\\n\\\\n* ``type`` (*Unicode string*) -- ``\\\\\\\"websocket.receive\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``bytes`` (*byte string*) -- The message content, if it was binary\\\\n  mode, or ``None``. Optional; if missing, it is equivalent to\\\\n  ``None``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``text`` (*Unicode string*) -- The message content, if it was text\\\\n  mode, or ``None``. Optional; if missing, it is equivalent to\\\\n  ``None``.\\\\n\\\\nExactly one of ``bytes`` or ``text`` must be non-``None``. One or both\\\\nkeys may be present, however.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nSend - ``send`` event\\\\n'''''''''''''''''''''\\\\n\\\\nSent by the application to send a data message to the client.\\\\n\\\\nKeys:\\\\n\\\\n* ``type`` (*Unicode string*) -- ``\\\\\\\"websocket.send\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``bytes`` (*byte string*) -- Binary message content, or ``None``.\\\\n   Optional; if missing, it is equivalent to ``None``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``text`` (*Unicode string*) -- Text message content, or ``None``.\\\\n   Optional; if missing, it is equivalent to ``None``.\\\\n\\\\nExactly one of ``bytes`` or ``text`` must be non-``None``. One or both\\\\nkeys may be present, however.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n.. _disconnect-receive-event-ws:\\\\n\\\\nDisconnect - ``receive`` event\\\\n''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''\\\\n\\\\nSent to the application when either connection to the client is lost, either from\\\\nthe client closing the connection, the server closing the connection, or loss of the\\\\nsocket.\\\\n\\\\nOnce you have received this event, you should expect future calls to ``send()``\\\\nto raise an exception, as described below. However, if you have highly\\\\nconcurrent code, you may find calls to ``send()`` erroring slightly before you\\\\nreceive this event.\\\\n\\\\nKeys:\\\\n\\\\n* ``type`` (*Unicode string*) -- ``\\\\\\\"websocket.disconnect\\\\\\\"``\\\\n\\\\n* ``code`` (*int*) -- The WebSocket close code, as per the WebSocket spec. If no code\\\\n  was received in the frame from the client, the server should set this to ``1005``\\\\n  (the default value in the WebSocket specification).\\\\n\\\\n* ``reason`` (*Unicode string*) -- A reason given for the disconnect, can\\\\n  be any string. Optional; if missing or ``None`` default is empty\\\\n  string.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nDisconnected Client - ``send`` exception\\\\n''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''\\\\n\\\\nIf ``send()`` is called on a closed connection the server should raise\\\\na server-specific subclass of ``OSError``. This is not guaranteed, however,\\\\nespecially on older ASGI server implementations (it was introduced in spec\\\\nversion 2.4).\\\\n\\\\nApplications may catch this exception and do cleanup work before\\\\nre-raising it or returning with no exception.\\\\n\\\\nServers must be prepared to catch this exception if they raised it and\\\\nshould not log it as an error in their server logs.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nClose - ``send`` event\\\\n''''''''''''''''''''''\\\\n\\\\nSent by the application to tell the server to close the connection.\\\\n\\\\nIf this is sent before the socket is accepted, the server\\\\nmust close the connection with a HTTP 403 error code\\\\n(Forbidden), and not complete the WebSocket handshake; this may present on some\\\\nbrowsers as a different WebSocket error code (such as 1006, Abnormal Closure).\\\\n\\\\nIf this is sent after the socket is accepted, the server must close the socket\\\\nwith the close code passed in the message (or 1000 if none is specified).\\\\n\\\\n* ``type`` (*Unicode string*) -- ``\\\\\\\"websocket.close\\\\\\\"``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``code`` (*int*) -- The WebSocket close code, as per the WebSocket\\\\n  spec.  Optional; if missing defaults to ``1000``.\\\\n\\\\n* ``reason`` (*Unicode string*) -- A reason given for the closure, can\\\\n  be any string. Optional; if missing or ``None`` default is empty\\\\n  string.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nWSGI Compatibility\\\\n------------------\\\\n\\\\nPart of the design of the HTTP portion of this spec is to make sure it\\\\naligns well with the WSGI specification, to ensure easy adaptability\\\\nbetween both specifications and the ability to keep using WSGI\\\\napplications with ASGI servers.\\\\n\\\\nWSGI applications, being synchronous, must be run in a threadpool in order\\\\nto be served, but otherwise their runtime maps onto the HTTP connection scope's\\\\nlifetime.\\\\n\\\\nThere is an almost direct mapping for the various special keys in\\\\nWSGI's ``environ`` variable to the ``http`` scope:\\\\n\\\\n* ``REQUEST_METHOD`` is the ``method``\\\\n* ``SCRIPT_NAME`` is ``root_path``\\\\n* ``PATH_INFO`` can be derived by stripping ``root_path`` from ``path``\\\\n* ``QUERY_STRING`` is ``query_string``\\\\n* ``CONTENT_TYPE`` can be extracted from ``headers``\\\\n* ``CONTENT_LENGTH`` can be extracted from ``headers``\\\\n* ``SERVER_NAME`` and ``SERVER_PORT`` are in ``server``\\\\n* ``REMOTE_HOST``/``REMOTE_ADDR`` and ``REMOTE_PORT`` are in ``client``\\\\n* ``SERVER_PROTOCOL`` is encoded in ``http_version``\\\\n* ``wsgi.url_scheme`` is ``scheme``\\\\n* ``wsgi.input`` is a ``StringIO`` based around the ``http.request`` messages\\\\n* ``wsgi.errors`` is directed by the wrapper as needed\\\\n\\\\nThe ``start_response`` callable maps similarly to ``http.response.start``:\\\\n\\\\n* The ``status`` argument becomes ``status``, with the reason phrase dropped.\\\\n* ``response_headers`` maps to ``headers``\\\\n\\\\nYielding content from the WSGI application maps to sending\\\\n``http.response.body`` messages.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nWSGI encoding differences\\\\n-------------------------\\\\n\\\\nThe WSGI specification (as defined in PEP 3333) specifies that all strings\\\\nsent to or from the server must be of the ``str`` type but only contain\\\\ncodepoints in the ISO-8859-1 (\\\\\\\"latin-1\\\\\\\") range. This was due to it originally\\\\nbeing designed for Python 2 and its different set of string types.\\\\n\\\\nThe ASGI HTTP and WebSocket specifications instead specify each entry of the\\\\n``scope`` dict as either a byte string or a Unicode string. HTTP, being an\\\\nolder protocol, is sometimes imperfect at specifying encoding, so some\\\\ndecisions of what is Unicode versus bytes may not be obvious.\\\\n\\\\n* ``path``: URLs can have both percent-encoded and UTF-8 encoded sections.\\\\n  Because decoding these is often done by the underlying server (or sometimes\\\\n  even proxies in the path), this is a Unicode string, fully decoded from both\\\\n  UTF-8 encoding and percent encodings.\\\\n\\\\n* ``headers``: These are byte strings of the exact byte sequences sent by the\\\\n  client/to be sent by the server. While modern HTTP standards say that headers\\\\n  should be ASCII, older ones did not and allowed a wider range of characters.\\\\n  Frameworks/applications should decode headers as they deem appropriate.\\\\n\\\\n* ``query_string``: Unlike the ``path``, this is not as subject to server\\\\n  interference and so is presented as its raw byte string version,\\\\n  percent-encoded.\\\\n\\\\n* ``root_path``: Unicode string to match ``path``.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nVersion History\\\\n---------------\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n* 2.0 (2017-11-28): Initial non-channel-layer based ASGI spec\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nCopyright\\\\n---------\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nThis document has been placed in the public domain.\\\\n\\\", \\\"excerpt_ranges\\\": [[0, 23566]], \\\"range_unit\\\": \\\"zero-based half-open characters in extracted text\\\", \\\"extracted_characters\\\": 23566, \\\"selected_characters\\\": 23566, \\\"extraction\\\": \\\"UTF-8 text\\\", \\\"selection_reason\\\": \\\"full extracted text fits allocation\\\"}, {\\\"path\\\": \\\"references/S-INT8/fulltext.txt\\\", \\\"sha256\\\": \\\"1137a01d16d677bc5d236a2fd4905a2fff8319b3f719494e51f1fb830176c3d4\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"source_original\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"=== PDF page 1 ===\\\\narXiv:1712.05877v1  [cs.LG]  15 Dec 2017\\\\nQuantization and Training of Neural Networks for Efﬁcient\\\\nInteger-Arithmetic-Only Inference\\\\nBenoit Jacob\\\\nSkirmantas Kligys\\\\nBo Chen\\\\nMenglong Zhu\\\\nMatthew Tang\\\\nAndrew Howard\\\\nHartwig Adam\\\\nDmitry Kalenichenko\\\\n{benoitjacob,skligys,bochen,menglong,\\\\nmttang,howarda,hadam,dkalenichenko}@google.com\\\\nGoogle Inc.\\\\nAbstract\\\\nThe rising popularity of intelligent mobile devices and\\\\nthe daunting computational cost of deep learning-based\\\\nmodels call for efﬁcient and accurate on-device inference\\\\nschemes. We propose a quantization scheme that allows\\\\ninference to be carried out using integer-only arithmetic,\\\\nwhich can be implemented more efﬁciently than ﬂoating\\\\npoint inference on commonly available integer-only hard-\\\\nware. We also co-design a training procedure to preserve\\\\nend-to-end model accuracy post quantization. As a result,\\\\nthe proposed quantization scheme improves the tradeoff be-\\\\ntween accuracy and on-device latency. The improvements\\\\nare signiﬁcant even on MobileNets, a model family known\\\\nfor run-time efﬁciency, and are demonstrated in ImageNet\\\\nclassiﬁcation and COCO detection on popular CPUs.\\\\n1. Introduction\\\\nCurrent state-of-the-art Convolutional Neural Networks\\\\n(CNNs) are not well suited for use on mobile devices. Since\\\\nthe advent of AlexNet [20], modern CNNs have primarily\\\\nbeen appraised according to classiﬁcation / detection accu-\\\\nracy. Thus network architectures have evolved without re-\\\\ngard to model complexity and computational efﬁciency. On\\\\nthe other hand, successful deployment of CNNs on mobile\\\\nplatforms such as smartphones, AR/VR devices (HoloLens,\\\\nDaydream), and drones require small model sizes to accom-\\\\nmodate limited on-device memory, and low latency to main-\\\\ntain user engagement. This has led to a burgeoning ﬁeld of\\\\nresearch that focuses on reducing the model size and infer-\\\\nence time of CNNs with minimal accuracy losses.\\\\nApproaches in this ﬁeld roughly fall into two cate-\\\\ngories. The ﬁrst category, exempliﬁed by MobileNet [10],\\\\nSqueezeNet [16], ShufﬂeNet [32], and DenseNet [11], de-\\\\nsigns novel network architectures that exploit computation\\\\n/ memory efﬁcient operations. The second category quan-\\\\ntizes the weights and / or activations of a CNN from 32\\\\nbit ﬂoating point into lower bit-depth representations. This\\\\nmethodology, embraced by approaches such as Ternary\\\\nweight networks (TWN [22]), Binary Neural Networks\\\\n(BNN [14]), XNOR-net [27], and more [8, 21, 26, 33, 34,\\\\n35], is the focus of our investigation. Despite their abun-\\\\ndance, current quantization approaches are lacking in two\\\\nrespects when it comes to trading off latency with accuracy.\\\\nFirst, prior approaches have not been evaluated on a\\\\nreasonable baseline architecture. The most common base-\\\\nline architectures, AlexNet [20], VGG [28] and GoogleNet\\\\n[29], are all over-parameterized by design in order to extract\\\\nmarginal accuracy improvements. Therefore, it is easy to\\\\nobtain sizable compression of these architectures, reducing\\\\nquantization experiments on these architectures to proof-\\\\nof-concepts at best. Instead, a more meaningful challenge\\\\nwould be to quantize model architectures that are already ef-\\\\nﬁcient at trading off latency with accuracy, e.g. MobileNets.\\\\nSecond, many quantization approaches do not deliver\\\\nveriﬁable efﬁciency improvements on real hardware. Ap-\\\\nproaches that quantize only the weights ([2, 4, 8, 33]) are\\\\nprimarily concerned with on-device storage and less with\\\\ncomputational efﬁciency. Notable exceptions are binary,\\\\nternary and bit-shift networks [14, 22, 27].\\\\nThese latter\\\\napproaches employ weights that are either 0 or powers of\\\\n2, which allow multiplication to be implemented by bit\\\\nshifts. However, while bit-shifts can be efﬁcient in cus-\\\\ntom hardware, they provide little beneﬁt on existing hard-\\\\nware with multiply-add instructions that, when properly\\\\nused (i.e. pipelined), are not more expensive than addi-\\\\ntions alone. Moreover, multiplications are only expensive\\\\nif the operands are wide, and the need to avoid multiplica-\\\\ntions diminishes with bit depth once both weights and acti-\\\\nvations are quantized. Notably, these approaches rarely pro-\\\\nvide on-device measurements to verify the promised timing\\\\nimprovements. More runtime-friendly approaches quantize\\\\nboth the weights and the activations into 1 bit representa-\\\\n1\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 2 ===\\\\nconv\\\\nweights\\\\nuint8\\\\ninput\\\\n+\\\\nbiases\\\\nuint32\\\\nReLU6\\\\noutput\\\\nuint8\\\\nuint32\\\\nuint8\\\\nuint8\\\\n(a) Integer-arithmetic-only inference\\\\nconv\\\\nwt quant\\\\nweights\\\\ninput\\\\n+\\\\nbiases\\\\nReLU6\\\\nact quant\\\\noutput\\\\n(b) Training with simulated quantization\\\\n10\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n80\\\\n160\\\\n320\\\\n40\\\\n50\\\\n60\\\\n70\\\\nLatency (ms)\\\\nTop 1 Accuracy\\\\nFloat\\\\n8-bit\\\\n(c) ImageNet latency-vs-accuracy tradeoff\\\\nFigure 1.1: Integer-arithmetic-only quantization. a) Integer-arithmetic-only inference of a convolution layer. With these approaches, both multiplica-\\\\ntions and additions can be implemented by efﬁcient bit-shift\\\\nand bit-count operations, which are showcased in custom\\\\nGPU kernels (BNN [14]). However, 1 bit quantization of-\\\\nten leads to substantial performance degradation, and may\\\\nbe overly stringent on model representation.\\\\nIn this paper we address the above issues by improving\\\\nthe latency-vs-accuracy tradeoffs of MobileNets on com-\\\\nmon mobile hardware. Our speciﬁc contributions are:\\\\n• We provide a quantization scheme (section 2.1) that\\\\nquantizesh both weights and activations as 8-bit integers,\\\\nand just a few parameters (bias vectors) as 32-bit integers.\\\\n• We provide a quantized inference framework that is ef-\\\\nﬁciently implementable on integer-arithmetic-only hard-\\\\nware such as the Qualcomm Hexagon (sections 2.2, 2.3),\\\\nand we describe an efﬁcient, accurate implementation on\\\\nARM NEON (Appendix B).\\\\n• We provide a quantized training framework (section 3)\\\\nco-designed with our quantized inference to minimize the\\\\nloss of accuracy from quantization on real models.\\\\n• We apply our frameworks to efﬁcient classiﬁcation and\\\\ndetection systems based on MobileNets and provide\\\\nbenchmark results on popular ARM CPUs (section 4)\\\\nthat show signiﬁcant improvements in the latency-vs-\\\\naccuracy tradeoffs for state-of-the-art MobileNet archi-\\\\ntectures, demonstrated in ImageNet classiﬁcation [3],\\\\nCOCO object detection [23], and other tasks.\\\\nOur work draws inspiration from [7], which leverages\\\\nlow-precision ﬁxed-point arithmetic to accelerate the train-\\\\ning speed of CNNs, and from [31], which uses 8-bit ﬁxed-\\\\npoint arithmetic to speed up inference on x86 CPUs. Our\\\\nquantization scheme focuses instead on improving the in-\\\\nference speed vs accuracy tradeoff on mobile CPUs.\\\\n2. Quantized Inference\\\\n2.1. Quantization scheme\\\\nIn this section, we describe our general quantization\\\\nscheme12, that is, the correspondence between the bit-\\\\nrepresentation of values (denoted q below, for “quantized\\\\nvalue”) and their interpretation as mathematical real num-\\\\nbers (denoted r below, for “real value”). Our quantization\\\\nscheme is implemented using integer-only arithmetic dur-\\\\ning inference and ﬂoating-point arithmetic during training,\\\\nwith both implementations maintaining a high degree of\\\\ncorrespondence with each other. We achieve this by ﬁrst\\\\nproviding a mathematically rigorous deﬁnition of our quan-\\\\ntization scheme, and separately adopting this scheme for\\\\nboth integer-arithmetic inference and ﬂoating-point train-\\\\ning.\\\\n1The quantization scheme described here is the one adopted in Tensor-\\\\nFlow Lite [5] and we will refer to speciﬁc parts of its code to illustrate\\\\naspects discussed below.\\\\n2We had earlier described this quantization scheme in the documen-\\\\ntation of gemmlowp [18]. That page may still be useful as an alternate\\\\ntreatment of some of the topics developed in this section, and for its self-\\\\ncontained example code.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 3 ===\\\\nA basic requirement of our quantization scheme is that it\\\\npermits efﬁcient implementation of all arithmetic using only\\\\ninteger arithmetic operations on the quantized values (we\\\\neschew implementations requiring lookup tables because\\\\nthese tend to perform poorly compared to pure arithmetic\\\\non SIMD hardware). This is equivalent to requiring that the\\\\nquantization scheme be an afﬁne mapping of integers q to\\\\nreal numbers r, i.e. of the form\\\\nr = S(q −Z)\\\\n(1)\\\\nfor some constants S and Z. Equation (1) is our quantiza-\\\\ntion scheme and the constants S and Z are our quantization\\\\nparameters. Our quantization scheme uses a single set of\\\\nquantization parameters for all values within each activa-\\\\ntions array and within each weights array; separate arrays\\\\nuse separate quantization parameters.\\\\nFor 8-bit quantization, q is quantized as an 8-bit integer\\\\n(for B-bit quantization, q is quantized as an B-bit integer).\\\\nSome arrays, typically bias vectors, are quantized as 32-bit\\\\nintegers, see section 2.4.\\\\nThe constant S (for “scale”) is an arbitrary positive real\\\\nnumber. It is typically represented in software as a ﬂoating-\\\\npoint quantity, like the real values r. Section 2.2 describes\\\\nmethods for avoiding the representation of such ﬂoating-\\\\npoint quantities in the inference workload.\\\\nThe constant Z (for “zero-point”) is of the same type\\\\nas quantized values q, and is in fact the quantized value q\\\\ncorresponding to the real value 0. This allows us to auto-\\\\nmatically meet the requirement that the real value r = 0 be\\\\nexactly representable by a quantized value. The motivation\\\\nfor this requirement is that efﬁcient implementation of neu-\\\\nral network operators often requires zero-padding of arrays\\\\naround boundaries.\\\\nOur discussion so far is summarized in the following\\\\nquantized buffer data structure3, with one instance of such a\\\\nbuffer existing for each activations array and weights array\\\\nin a neural network. We use C++ syntax because it allows\\\\nthe unambiguous conveyance of types.\\\\ntemplate<typename QType>\\\\n// e.g. QType=uint8\\\\nstruct QuantizedBuffer {\\\\nvector<QType> q;\\\\n// the quantized values\\\\nfloat S;\\\\n// the scale\\\\nQType Z;\\\\n// the zero-point\\\\n};\\\\n2.2. We empirically ﬁnd\\\\nit to always be in the interval (0, 1), and can therefore ex-\\\\npress it in the normalized form\\\\nM = 2−nM0\\\\n(6)\\\\nwhere M0 is in the interval [0.5, 1) and n is a non-negative\\\\ninteger. The normalized multiplier M0 now lends itself well\\\\nto being expressed as a ﬁxed-point multiplier (e.g. int16 or\\\\nint32 depending on hardware capability). For example, if\\\\nint32 is used, the integer representing M0 is the int32 value\\\\nnearest to 231M0. Since M0 ⩾0.5, this value is always at\\\\nleast 230 and will therefore always have at least 30 bits of\\\\nrelative accuracy. Multiplication by M0 can thus be imple-\\\\nmented as a ﬁxed-point multiplication4. Meanwhile, multi-\\\\nplication by 2−n can be implemented with an efﬁcient bit-\\\\nshift, albeit one that needs to have correct round-to-nearest\\\\nbehavior, an issue that we return to in Appendix B.\\\\n2.3. Efﬁcient handling of zero-points\\\\nIn order to efﬁciently implement the evaluation of Equa-\\\\ntion (4) without having to perform 2N 3 subtractions and\\\\n4The computation discussed in this section is implemented in Tensor-\\\\nFlow Lite [5] reference code for a fully-connected layer.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 4 ===\\\\nwithout having to expand the operands of the multiplication\\\\ninto 16-bit integers, we ﬁrst notice that by distributing the\\\\nmultiplication in Equation (4), we can rewrite it as\\\\nq(i,k)\\\\n3\\\\n= Z3 + M\\\\n\\\\nNZ1Z2 −Z1a(k)\\\\n2\\\\n−Z2¯a(i)\\\\n1 +\\\\nN\\\\nX\\\\nj=1\\\\nq(i,j)\\\\n1\\\\nq(j,k)\\\\n2\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n(7)\\\\nwhere\\\\na(k)\\\\n2\\\\n:=\\\\nN\\\\nX\\\\nj=1\\\\nq(j,k)\\\\n2\\\\n, ¯a(i)\\\\n1\\\\n:=\\\\nN\\\\nX\\\\nj=1\\\\nq(i,j)\\\\n1\\\\n.\\\\n(8)\\\\nEach a(k)\\\\n2\\\\nor ¯a(i)\\\\n1 takes only N additions to compute, so they\\\\ncollectively take only 2N 2 additions. Implementation of a typical fused layer\\\\nWe continue the discussion of section 2.3, but now ex-\\\\nplicitly deﬁne the data types of all quantities involved, and\\\\nmodify the quantized matrix multiplication (7) to merge\\\\nthe bias-addition and activation function evaluation directly\\\\ninto it. This fusing of whole layers into a single operation\\\\nis not only an optimization. As we must reproduce in in-\\\\nference code the same arithmetic that is used in training,\\\\nthe granularity of fused operators in inference code (taking\\\\nan 8-bit quantized input and producing an 8-bit quantized\\\\noutput) must match the placement of “fake quantization”\\\\noperators in the training graph (section 3).\\\\nFor our implementation on ARM and x86 CPU ar-\\\\nchitectures, we use the gemmlowp library [18], whose\\\\nGemmWithOutputPipeline entry point provides sup-\\\\nports the fused operations that we now describe5.\\\\n5The discussion in this section is implemented in TensorFlow Lite [5]\\\\nfor e.g. a Convolutional operator (reference code is self-contained, opti-\\\\nmized code calls into gemmlowp [18]).\\\\nWe take the q1 matrix to be the weights, and the q2 matrix\\\\nto be the activations. Both the weights and activations are\\\\nof type uint8 (we could have equivalently chosen int8, with\\\\nsuitably modiﬁed zero-points). Accumulating products of\\\\nuint8 values requires a 32-bit accumulator, and we choose a\\\\nsigned type for the accumulator for a reason that will soon\\\\nbecome clear. The sum in (9) is thus of the form:\\\\nint32 += uint8 * uint8.\\\\n(10)\\\\nIn order to have the quantized bias-addition be the addition\\\\nof an int32 bias into this int32 accumulator, the bias-vector\\\\nis quantized such that: it uses int32 as its quantized data\\\\ntype; it uses 0 as its quantization zero-point Zbias; and its\\\\nquantization scale Sbias is the same as that of the accumu-\\\\nlators, which is the product of the scales of the weights and\\\\nof the input activations. In the notation of section 2.3,\\\\nSbias = S1S2, Zbias = 0.\\\\n(11)\\\\nAlthough the bias-vectors are quantized as 32-bit values,\\\\nthey account for only a tiny fraction of the parameters in a\\\\nneural network. Furthermore, the use of higher precision\\\\nfor bias vectors meets a real need: as each bias-vector entry\\\\nis added to many output activations, any quantization error\\\\nin the bias-vector tends to act as an overall bias (i.e. an error\\\\nterm with nonzero mean), which must be avoided in order\\\\nto preserve good end-to-end neural network accuracy6.\\\\nWith the ﬁnal value of the int32 accumulator, there re-\\\\nmain three things left to do: scale down to the ﬁnal scale\\\\nused by the 8-bit output activations, cast down to uint8 and\\\\napply the activation function to yield the ﬁnal 8-bit output\\\\nactivation.\\\\nThe down-scaling corresponds to multiplication by the\\\\nmultiplier M in equation (7). As explained in section 2.2, it\\\\nis implemented as a ﬁxed-point multiplication by a normal-\\\\nized multiplier M0 and a rounding bit-shift. Afterwards, we\\\\nperform a saturating cast to uint8, saturating to the range\\\\n[0, 255].\\\\nWe focus on activation functions that are mere clamps,\\\\ne.g. ReLU, ReLU6. Mathematical functions are discussed\\\\nin appendix A.1 and we do not currently fuse them into such\\\\nlayers. Thus, the only thing that our fused activation func-\\\\ntions need to do is to further clamp the uint8 value to some\\\\nsub-interval of [0, 255] before storing the ﬁnal uint8 output\\\\nactivation. In practice, the quantized training process (sec-\\\\ntion 3) tends to learn to make use of the whole output uint8\\\\n[0, 255] interval so that the activation function no longer\\\\ndoes anything, its effect being subsumed in the clamping\\\\nto [0, 255] implied in the saturating cast to uint8.\\\\n6The quantization of bias-vectors discussed here is implemented here\\\\nin the TensorFlow Lite [5] Converter.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 5 ===\\\\n3. Training with simulated quantization\\\\nA common approach to training quantized networks is\\\\nto train in ﬂoating point and then quantize the resulting\\\\nweights (sometimes with additional post-quantization train-\\\\ning for ﬁne-tuning). We found that this approach works\\\\nsufﬁciently well for large models with considerable repre-\\\\nsentational capacity, but leads to signiﬁcant accuracy drops\\\\nfor small models. Common failure modes for simple post-\\\\ntraining quantization include: 1) large differences (more\\\\nthan 100×) in ranges of weights for different output chan-\\\\nnels (section 2 mandates that all channels of the same layer\\\\nbe quantized to the same resolution, which causes weights\\\\nin channels with smaller ranges to have much higher relative\\\\nerror) and 2) outlier weight values that make all remaining\\\\nweights less precise after quantization.\\\\nWe propose an approach that simulates quantization ef-\\\\nfects in the forward pass of training. Backpropagation still\\\\nhappens as usual, and all weights and biases are stored in\\\\nﬂoating point so that they can be easily nudged by small\\\\namounts.\\\\nThe forward propagation pass however simu-\\\\nlates quantized inference as it will happen in the inference\\\\nengine, by implementing in ﬂoating-point arithmetic the\\\\nrounding behavior of the quantization scheme that we in-\\\\ntroduced in section 2:\\\\n• Weights are quantized before they are convolved with\\\\nthe input. If batch normalization (see [17]) is used for\\\\nthe layer, the batch normalization parameters are “folded\\\\ninto” the weights before quantization, see section 3.2.\\\\n• Activations are quantized at points where they would be\\\\nduring inference, e.g. after the activation function is ap-\\\\nplied to a convolutional or fully connected layer’s output,\\\\nor after a bypass connection adds or concatenates the out-\\\\nputs of several layers together such as in ResNets.\\\\nFor each layer, quantization is parameterized by the\\\\nnumber of quantization levels and clamping range, and is\\\\nperformed by applying point-wise the quantization function\\\\nq deﬁned as follows:\\\\nclamp(r; a, b) := min (max(x, a), b)\\\\ns(a, b, n) := b −a\\\\nn −1\\\\nq(r; a, b, n) :=\\\\n\\\\u0016clamp(r; a, b) −a\\\\ns(a, b, n)\\\\n\\\\u0019\\\\ns(a, b, n) + a,\\\\n(12)\\\\nwhere r is a real-valued number to be quantized, [a; b] is the\\\\nquantization range, n is the number of quantization levels,\\\\nand ⌊·⌉denotes rounding to the nearest integer. n is ﬁxed\\\\nfor all layers in our experiments, e.g. n = 28 = 256 for 8\\\\nbit quantization.\\\\n3.1. Learning quantization ranges\\\\nQuantization ranges are treated differently for weight\\\\nquantization vs. activation quantization:\\\\n• For weights, the basic idea is simply to set a := min w,\\\\nb := max w. We apply a minor tweak to this so that\\\\nthe weights, once quantized as int8 values, only range\\\\nin [−127, 127] and never take the value −128, as this en-\\\\nables a substantial optimization opportunity (for more de-\\\\ntails, see Appendix B).\\\\n• For activations, ranges depend on the inputs to the net-\\\\nwork. To estimate the ranges, we collect [a; b] ranges\\\\nseen on activations during training and then aggregate\\\\nthem via exponential moving averages (EMA) with the\\\\nsmoothing parameter being close to 1 so that observed\\\\nranges are smoothed across thousands of training steps.\\\\nGiven signiﬁcant delay in the EMA updating activation\\\\nranges when the ranges shift rapidly, we found it useful\\\\nto completely disable activation quantization at the start\\\\nof training (say, for 50 thousand to 2 million steps). This\\\\nallows the network to enter a more stable state where ac-\\\\ntivation quantization ranges do not exclude a signiﬁcant\\\\nfraction of values.\\\\nIn both cases, the boundaries [a; b] are nudged so that\\\\nvalue 0.0 is exactly representable as an integer z(a, b, n)\\\\nafter quantization. As a result, the learned quantization pa-\\\\nrameters map to the scale S and zero-point Z in equation 1:\\\\nS = s(a, b, n), Z = z(a, b, n)\\\\n(13)\\\\nBelow we depict simulated quantization assuming that\\\\nthe computations of a neural network are captured as a Ten-\\\\nsorFlow graph [1]. A typical workﬂow is described in Al-\\\\ngorithm 1. Discussion\\\\nWe propose a quantization scheme that relies only on\\\\ninteger arithmetic to approximate the ﬂoating-point com-\\\\nputations in a neural network. Training that simulates the\\\\neffect of quantization helps to restore model accuracy to\\\\nnear-identical levels as the original. In addition to the 4×\\\\nreduction of model size, inference efﬁciency is improved\\\\nvia ARM NEON-based implementations.\\\\nThe improve-\\\\nment advances the state-of-the-art tradeoff between latency\\\\non common ARM CPUs and the accuracy of popular com-\\\\nputer vision models. The synergy between our quantiza-\\\\ntion scheme and efﬁcient architecture design suggests that\\\\ninteger-arithmetic-only inference could be a key enabler\\\\nthat propels visual recognition technologies into the real-\\\\ntime and low-end phone market.\\\\nReferences\\\\n[1] M.
